A comet is an icy body orbiting the Sun, composed of frozen volatiles like water ice, methane, ammonia, and carbon dioxide, along with dust. When a comet's elliptical orbit brings it close to the Sun, solar heating causes its ices to sublimate, forming a luminous coma, a halo of gas and dust, and a spectacular tail that can stretch millions of kilometers. Comets have been observed and interpreted as omens for millennia; modern astronomy reveals them as preserved relics of the early solar system and crucial sources of information about its formation.

Comets originate from two reservoirs. The Kuiper Belt is the source of short-period comets with orbital periods under two hundred years. The Oort Cloud is the source of long-period and hyperbolic comets from the outer solar system. A comet consists of a solid nucleus, typically a few kilometers across, a coma of dust and gas surrounding it, and a tail always pointing away from the Sun due to solar wind and radiation pressure.

Halley's Comet, the most famous, returns every approximately seventy-six years. It was observed and recorded by ancient civilizations, and its next appearance is predicted for twenty sixty-one. Comets deposit dusty trails in their orbits. When Earth passes through these trails, the particles burn up in the atmosphere, creating meteor showers.

Comet Shoemaker-Levy nine collided with Jupiter in nineteen ninety-four, leaving visible impact scars and providing direct evidence of catastrophic bombardment in the solar system. The European Space Agency's Rosetta mission orbited Comet sixty-seven P Churyumov-Gerasimenko and landed the Philae probe on its nucleus, revealing surprising geological complexity.

Historically, comets were often regarded as harbingers of disaster or divine signs. Their predictability, once orbital mechanics advanced, eliminated superstition.
